```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
ords <- read_csv(file.path(res, "ordinations.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
perm <- read_csv(file.path(res, "permanova.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
scree <- read_csv(file.path(res, "scree.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cs <- read_csv("../3-differential/results/contrast_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_genes_outcome <- cs$n_sig[cs$contrast == "genes_by_outcome"]

ord_fig <- function(which_ord, colour_by, title = NULL, legend = "right") {
  d <- ords |> filter(ordination == which_ord)
  ggplot(d, aes(axis1, axis2, colour = .data[[colour_by]])) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
    labs(x = "axis 1", y = "axis 2", colour = NULL,
         title = title %||% which_ord) +
    theme(legend.position = legend)
}
`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x)) y else x
r2 <- function(tbl, trm) {
  v <- perm$R2[perm$table == tbl & perm$term == trm]
  scales::percent(v, 0.1)
}

# toy pair of samples for the distance slide (counts invented for illustration)
toy <- tibble(
  species = c("L. crispatus", "G. vaginalis", "A. vaginae", "Prevotella", "Sneathia"),
  A = c(900, 60, 30, 10, 0),
  B = c(300, 400, 200, 0, 100)
)
pA <- toy$A / sum(toy$A); pB <- toy$B / sum(toy$B)
toy_bray <- sum(abs(pA - pB)) / sum(pA + pB)
toy_jac <- 1 - sum(toy$A > 0 & toy$B > 0) / sum(toy$A > 0 | toy$B > 0)
clr <- function(x) log(x) - mean(log(x))
toy_ait <- sqrt(sum((clr(toy$A + 1) - clr(toy$B + 1))^2))

term_labels <- c(community = "community", outcome = "birth outcome",
                 time_point = "visit", rnaseq_batch = "RNA-seq batch")
```

## From one feature to whole samples {.center}

Yesterday you tested one feature at a time. Today the question is **how similar
two whole samples are**.

. . .

That gives one number per pair of samples, and then a picture of all of them at
once.

## A distance matrix

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
set.seed(3)
n <- 12
m <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(n * 4), n)))
as_tibble(m, .name_repair = ~ paste0("S", seq_along(.x))) |>
  mutate(row = paste0("S", row_number())) |>
  pivot_longer(-row) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, paste0("S", 1:n)),
         name = factor(name, paste0("S", 1:n))) |>
  ggplot(aes(name, fct_rev(row), fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = pal[["navy"]]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "distance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

This toy has 12 samples. Ours has 471, which makes 110,685 pairs. The diagonal
is zero, the matrix is symmetric, and there is nothing else in it.

## Choosing a distance

:::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.8em"}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Bray-Curtis works on proportions and measures how much of the two
  communities overlaps. Abundant features dominate the answer.
- Jaccard works on presence and absence: the share of features present in
  either sample that are present in both. Abundance is ignored entirely.
- Aitchison is Euclidean distance on centred log-ratios, built for data where
  only the ratios between features mean anything.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Two invented samples:

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(toy, align = "lrr")
```

::: {.fragment}
| distance | A to B |
|---|---|
| Bray-Curtis | `r round(toy_bray, 2)` |
| Jaccard | `r round(toy_jac, 2)` |
| Aitchison, pseudocount 1 | `r round(toy_ait, 2)` |
:::
:::
::::

## The microViz pipeline

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(microViz)
source("R/count_tables.R")

as_counts(table = "microbiome") |>
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "species") |>   # knob 1: the transform
  dist_calc("bray") |>                             # knob 2: the distance
  ord_calc("PCoA") |>                              # knob 3: the layout
  ord_plot(colour = "community")
```

. . .

| transform | distance |
|---|---|
| `"identity"` on proportions | `"bray"` |
| `"binary"` | `"jaccard"` |
| `"clr"` | `"euclidean"` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

## The species ordination under each distance

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 5.6
p1 <- ord_fig("species / Bray-Curtis", "community", "Bray-Curtis", "none")
p2 <- ord_fig("species / Jaccard", "community", "Jaccard", "none")
p3 <- ord_fig("species / Aitchison", "community", "Aitchison", "bottom")
(p1 + p2 + p3) &
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]]))
```

All three plots come from the same table. Which would you put in a paper, and
how would you defend it?

## Variation held by each axis

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.6
scree |>
  filter(axis <= 8) |>
  mutate(table = factor(table, c("species / Bray-Curtis", "genes / Aitchison"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(axis), variance_share, fill = table)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`species / Bray-Curtis` = pal[["teal"]],
                               `genes / Aitchison` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  facet_wrap(~table) +
  labs(x = "axis", y = "share of variation") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The first two axes of the species ordination hold about
`r scales::percent(sum(scree$variance_share[scree$table == "species / Bray-Curtis" & scree$axis <= 2]), 1)`
of the variation. For the genes, about
`r scales::percent(sum(scree$variance_share[scree$table == "genes / Aitchison" & scree$axis <= 2]), 1)`.

## Colour the same plot by the thing you care about

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
a <- ord_fig("species / Bray-Curtis", "community", "by community", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]]))
b <- ord_fig("species / Bray-Curtis", "outcome", "by birth outcome", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(preterm = pal[["orange"]], term = pal[["navy"]]))
a + b
```

. . .

Community type splits the plot cleanly. Birth outcome is the label you actually
care about, and by eye you cannot see it.

## Testing a label with PERMANOVA

```{r}
#| eval: false
as_counts(table = "microbiome") |>
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "species") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  dist_permanova(variables = c("community", "outcome", "time_point", "rnaseq_batch"),
                 n_perms = 999, by = "margin")
```

PERMANOVA asks: if I shuffled this label across samples, how often would the
groups end up this far apart by chance?

. . .

`R2` is the share of the total variation that the label explains.

## The species table

::::: {style="font-size: 0.88em"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
perm |>
  filter(table == "species / Bray-Curtis", !term %in% c("Residual", "Total")) |>
  transmute(term, R2 = scales::percent(R2, 0.1), `F` = round(`F`, 1),
            p = p_value) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

::: {.incremental}
- Community type explains `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "community")`. Enormous,
  and expected, since we defined it from this table.
- Visit explains `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "time_point")`. These
  communities move over pregnancy.
- Birth outcome explains `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "outcome")`. Significant
  and tiny.
- The **RNA** sequencing batch explains `r r2("species / Bray-Curtis", "rnaseq_batch")`,
  not significant. It should not touch the 16S data.
:::

:::::

## Now the gene table

The species code from this morning:

```{r}
#| eval: false
as_counts(table = "microbiome") |>
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "species") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA") |>
  ord_plot(colour = "community")
```

The gene version filters out rare genes and swaps the transform, rank and
distance. The rest is the same:

```{r}
#| eval: false
as_counts(table = "rnaseq", min_count = 10, min_samples = 100) |>
  tax_transform("clr", rank = "symbol") |>
  dist_calc("euclidean") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA") |>
  ord_plot(colour = "community")
```

## Gene ordination: community, outcome, batch

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 6.6
g1 <- ord_fig("genes / Aitchison", "community", "by community", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]]))
g2 <- ord_fig("genes / Aitchison", "outcome", "by birth outcome", "bottom") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(preterm = pal[["orange"]], term = pal[["navy"]]))
g3 <- ords |> filter(ordination == "genes / Aitchison") |>
  ggplot(aes(axis1, axis2, colour = rnaseq_batch)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(B1 = pal[["navy"]], B2 = pal[["gold"]])) +
  labs(x = "axis 1", y = "axis 2", colour = NULL, title = "by sequencing batch") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
g1 + g2 + g3
```

## The uncomfortable table

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
perm |>
  filter(!term %in% c("Residual", "Total")) |>
  mutate(term = factor(term_labels[term], rev(term_labels)),
         table = factor(table, c("species / Bray-Curtis", "genes / Aitchison")),
         lab = paste0(scales::percent(R2, 0.1), "  (p = ", p_value, ")")) |>
  ggplot(aes(R2, term, fill = term == "RNA-seq batch")) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), hjust = -0.08, size = 5.5) +
  facet_wrap(~table, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(1), breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(3),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.8))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pal[["grey"]], `TRUE` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  labs(x = "R2, share of variation explained", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"))
```

. . .

In the gene table, the sequencing batch explains as much as the biology does,
and it is just as significant.

## Dealing with batch {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- The ordination did not show it. PERMANOVA measured it.
- Put it in the model: `~ rnaseq_batch + outcome`.
- If batch is confounded with your groups, nothing fixes it, so check that first.
- None of this is possible if nobody wrote the batch down.
:::

## Significant and small

Birth outcome explains `r r2("genes / Aitchison", "outcome")` of the variation
in the gene table, p = 0.005.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 2.4
perm |>
  filter(table == "genes / Aitchison", term != "Total") |>
  mutate(part = case_when(term == "outcome" ~ "birth outcome",
                          term == "Residual" ~ "unexplained",
                          TRUE ~ "other labels"),
         part = factor(part, c("birth outcome", "other labels", "unexplained"))) |>
  group_by(part) |>
  summarise(R2 = sum(R2)) |>
  arrange(part) |>
  mutate(xmax = cumsum(R2), xmin = xmax - R2, mid = (xmin + xmax) / 2,
         lab = paste(part, scales::percent(R2, 0.1)),
         ylab = c(1.35, -0.35, 0.5), vj = c(0, 1, 0.5),
         hj = c(0, 0, 0.5), xl = c(0, 0.0, 0.55)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = part)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = xl, y = ylab, label = lab, vjust = vj, hjust = hj), size = 7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(unexplained = "#eeeeee", `other labels` = pal[["grey"]],
                               `birth outcome` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.8, 1.8), clip = "off") +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

. . .

Yesterday the same comparison gave `r scales::comma(n_genes_outcome)` significant genes.

. . .

Both results hold. Many genes each shift a little, and small shifts in many
genes still add up to a small share of a very large amount of variation. We come
back to this on Friday.
